```python
"""
Dynamic host file management.
"""
import docker
from subprocess import call
import re


def refresh():
    """
    Ensure that all running containers have a valid entry in /etc/hosts.
    """
    containers = docker.containers()
    hosts = '\n'.join(['%s %s' % (c.address, c.domain) for c in [d for d in containers if d.running]])
    hosts = '# DORK START\n%s\n# DORK END' % hosts

    expr = re.compile('# DORK START\n(.*\n)*# DORK END')
    with open('/etc/hosts', 'r') as f:
        content = f.read()

    if len(expr.findall(content)) > 0:
        content = expr.sub(hosts, content)
    else:
        content += hosts + '\n'

    with open('/etc/hosts', 'w') as f:
        f.write(content)
    call(['sudo', 'service', 'dnsmasq', 'restart'])

```

```python
from collections import OrderedDict

from graphql.type.definition import GraphQLObjectType
from marshmallow import Schema, SchemaOpts

from polygraph.utils.trim_docstring import trim_docstring


class ObjectTypeOpts(SchemaOpts):
    def __init__(self, meta, **kwargs):
        SchemaOpts.__init__(self, meta, **kwargs)
        self.name = getattr(meta, 'name', None)
        self.description = getattr(meta, 'name', None)


class ObjectType(Schema):
    OPTIONS_CLASS = ObjectTypeOpts

    def __init__(self, only=(), exclude=(), prefix='', strict=None,
                 many=False, context=None, load_only=(), dump_only=(),
                 partial=False):
        super().__init__(only, exclude, prefix, strict,
                         many, context, load_only, dump_only, partial)
        self._name = self.opts.name or self.__class__.__name__
        self._description = self.opts.description or trim_docstring(self.__doc__)

    def build_definition(self):
        field_map = OrderedDict()
        for fieldname, field in self.fields.items():
            field_map[fieldname] = field.build_definition()
        return GraphQLObjectType(name=self._name,
                                 fields=field_map,
                                 description=self._description)
```

```python
def get_supported_currencies(config: "GatewayConfig", gateway_name: str) -> List[str]:

    if not supp_currencies:

        warnings.warn(
            f"Default currency used for {gateway_name}. "
            "DEFAULT_CURRENCY setting is deprecated, "
```

    47	A Flask extension is available for initializing and configuring Honeybadger: `honeybadger.contrib.flask.FlaskHoneybadger`. The extension adds the following information to reported exceptions:

    59	- (Optionally) Reset honeybadger context after each request.

   129	## Logging
   130	
   131	By default, Honeybadger uses the `logging.NullHandler` for logging so it doesn't make any assumptions about your logging setup. In Django, add a `honeybadger` section to your `LOGGING` config to enable Honeybadger logging. For example:

   141	            'filename': '/path/to/django/debug.log',
   142	        },
   143	    },
   144	    'loggers': {
   145	        'honeybadger': {
   146	            'handlers': ['file'],
   147	            'level': 'DEBUG',
   148	            'propagate': True,
   149	        },
   150	    },
   151	}

   163	To set configuration options, use the `honeybadger.configure` method, like so:

   170

   172	
   173	|  Name | Type | Default | Example | Environment variable |
   174	| ----- | ---- | ------- | ------- | -------------------- |
   175	| api_key | `str` | `""` | `"badgers"` | `HONEYBADGER_API_KEY` |
   176	| project_root | `str` | The current working directory | `"/path/to/project"` | `HONEYBADGER_PROJECT_ROOT` |
   177	| environment | `str` | `"production"` | `"staging"` | `HONEYBADGER_ENVIRONMENT` |

   185	### `honeybadger.set_context`: Set global context data

   187	This method allows you to send additional information to the Honeybadger API to assist in debugging. This method sets global context data and is additive  - eg. every time you call it, it adds to the existing set unless you call `reset_context`, documented below.

   191	```python
   192	from honeybadger import honeybadger

   196	### `honeybadger.reset_context`: Clear global context data
   197	
   198	This method clears the global context dictionary.
   199	
   200	#### Examples:

   207	### `honeybadger.context`: Python context manager interface

   209	What if you don't want to set global context data? You can use Python context managers to set case-specific contextual information.

   211	#### Examples:
   212	
   213	```python
   214	# from a Django view
   215	from honeybadger import honeybadger
   216	def my_view(request):
   217	  with honeybadger.context(user_email=request.POST.get('user_email', None)):
   218	    form = UserForm(request.POST)
   219	    ...
   220	```

   222	### `honeybadger.configure`: Specify additional configuration options
   223	
   224	Allows you to configure honeybadger within your code. Accepts any of the above-listed configuration options as keyword arguments.
   225	
   226	#### Example:
   227	
   228	```python
   229	honeybadger.configure(api_key='myapikey', project_root='/home/dave/crywolf-django')

   234	In cases where you'd like to manually send error notices to Honeybadger, this is what you're looking for. You can either pass it an exception as the first argument, or an `error_class`/`error_message` pair of keyword arguments. You can also pass it a custom context dictionary which will get merged with the global context.

   243	except KeyError, exc:

### What was wrong?

In certain situations, web3 will raise ImportErrors on python 3.12 if the `setuptools` package is not installed. _In particular, this happens inside a  fresh Python 3.12 venv._ The `setuptools` package automatically installs the `pkg_resources` package, which is used in web3 [here](https://github.com/ethereum/web3.py/blob/8f853f5841fd62187bce0c9f17be75627104ca43/web3/__init__.py#L25). This used to work fine in older Python versions. However, according to the [new changes in 3.12](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.12.html):

> gh-95299: Do not pre-install setuptools in virtual environments created with venv. This means that distutils, setuptools, pkg_resources, and easy_install will no longer available by default; to access these run pip install setuptools in the activated virtual environment.

This means that the pkg_resources package is no longer accessible which causes this error.

Among other things, this scenario can occur inside tox tests for projects that have the `web3` package installed and are configured to test against 3.12. This causes such tests to immediately fail because of the ImportError. The workaround, installing setuptools after the venv created, causes unnecessarily long test times, adding about 3 minutes to the run time.

### How can it be fixed?

Given that web3's use of setuptools/pkg_resources is limited to just getting the version number, this should be trivial to fix. Why not open the file with built-in functions such as `open()` and parse it for the version number? I don't think that `web3` should continue to depend on setuptools.
</issue_description>

    24	---------------
    25	
    26	``` python
    27	from CHAID import Tree
    28	
    29	## create the data
    30	ndarr = np.array(([1, 2, 3] * 5) + ([2, 2, 3] * 5)).reshape(10, 3)
    31	df = pd.DataFrame(ndarr)
    32	df.columns = ['a', 'b', 'c']
    33	arr = np.array(([1] * 5) + ([2] * 5))
    34	df['d'] = arr
    35	
    36	>>> df
    37	   a  b  c  d
    38	0  1  2  3  1
    39	1  1  2  3  1
    40	2  1  2  3  1
    41	3  1  2  3  1
    42	4  1  2  3  1
    43	5  2  2  3  2
    44	6  2  2  3  2
    45	7  2  2  3  2
    46	8  2  2  3  2
    47	9  2  2  3  2
    48	
    49	## set the CHAID input parameters
    50	independent_variable_columns = ['a', 'b', 'c']
    51	dep_variable = 'd'
    52	
    53	## create the Tree via pandas
    54	tree = Tree.from_pandas_df(df, dict(zip(independent_variable_columns, ['nominal'] * 3)), dep_variable)
    55	## create the same tree, but without pandas helper
    56	tree = Tree.from_numpy(ndarr, arr, split_titles=['a', 'b', 'c'], min_child_node_size=5)
    57	## create the same tree using the tree constructor
    58	cols = [
    59	  NominalColumn(ndarr[:,0], name='a')
    60	  NominalColumn(ndarr[:,1], name='b')
    61	  NominalColumn(ndarr[:,2], name='c')
    62	]

    64

    68	└── ([2], {1: 0, 2: 5}, <Invalid Chaid Split>)

    79

    91	Creating a Tree using Bartlett's or Levene's Significance Test for Continuous Variables
    92	----------
    93	
    94	When the dependent variable is continuous, the chi-squared test does not work due to very low frequencies of values across subgroups. As a consequence, and because the F-test is very susceptible to deviations from normality, the normality of the dependent set is determined and [Bartlett's test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartlett%27s_test) for significance is used when the data is normally distributed (although the subgroups may not necessarily be so) or [Levene's test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levene%27s_test) is used when the data is non-normal.
    95	
    96	``` python
    97	from CHAID import Tree
    98	
    99	## create the data
   100	ndarr = np.array(([1, 2, 3] * 5) + ([2, 2, 3] * 5)).reshape(10, 3)
   101	df = pd.DataFrame(ndarr)
   102	df.columns = ['a', 'b', 'c']
   103	df['d'] = np.random.normal(300, 100, 10)
   104	independent_variable_columns = ['a', 'b', 'c']
   105	dep_variable = 'd'
   106	
   107	>>> df
   108	   a  b  c           d
   109	0  1  2  3  262.816747
   110	1  1  2  3  240.139085
   111	2  1  2  3  204.224083
   112	3  1  2  3  231.024752
   113	4  1  2  3  263.176338
   114	5  2  2  3  440.371621
   115	6  2  2  3  221.762452
   116	7  2  2  3  197.290268
   117	8  2  2  3  275.925549
   118	9  2  2  3  238.471850
   119	
   120	## create the Tree via pandas
   121	tree = Tree.from_pandas_df(df, dict(zip(independent_variable_columns, ['nominal'] * 3)), dep_variable, dep_variable_type='continuous')
   122	
   123	## print the tree (though not enough power to split)
   124	>>> tree.print_tree()
   125	([], {'s.t.d': 86.562258585515579, 'mean': 297.52027436303212}, <Invalid Chaid Split>)
   126	```
   127	
   128	Parameters
   129	----------
   130	* `df`: Pandas DataFrame
   131	* `i_variables: Dict<string, string>`: Independent variable column names as keys and the type as the values (nominal or ordinal)
   132	* `d_variable: String`: Dependent variable column name
   133	* `opts: {}`:
   134	  * `alpha_merge: Float (default = 0.05)`: If the respective test for a given pair of predictor categories is not statistically significant as defined by an `alpha_merge` value, the least significant predictor categories are merged and the splitting of the node is attempted with the newly formed categories
   135	  * `max_depth: Integer (default = 2)`: The maximum depth of the tree
   136	  * `min_parent_node_size: Float (default = 30)`: The minimum number of respondents required for a split to occur on a particular node
   137	  * `min_child_node_size: Float (default = 0)`: If the split of a node results in a child node whose node size is less than `min_child_node_size`, child nodes that have too few cases (as with this minimum) will merge with the most similar child node as measured by the largest of the p-values. However, if the resulting number of child nodes is 1, the node will not be split.
   138	  * `split_threshold: Float (default = 0)`: The split threshold when bucketing root node surrogate splits
   139	  * `weight: String (default = None)`: The name of the weight column
   140	  * `dep_variable_type (default = categorical, other_options = continuous)`: Whether the dependent variable is 'categorical' or 'continuous'

   226	├── (['female'], {0: 127, 1: 339}, (embarked, p=9.17624191599e-07, score=24.0936494474, groups=[['C', '<missing>'], ['Q', 'S']]), dof=1))

   233	
   234	as show above. The first line is the root node, all the data is present in this node. The the vertical bars originating from a node represents paths to that node's children.
   235	
   236	Running `tree.tree_store` will give you a list of all the nodes in the tree:
   237	
   238	``` python
   239	[
   240	  ([], {0: 809, 1: 500}, (sex, p=1.47145310169e-81, score=365.886947811, groups=[['female'], ['male']]), dof=1)),
   241	  (['female'], {0: 127, 1: 339}, (embarked, p=9.17624191599e-07, score=24.0936494474, groups=[['C', '<missing>'], ['Q', 'S']]), dof=1)),
   242	  (['C', '<missing>'], {0: 11, 1: 104}, <Invalid Chaid Split>), (['Q', 'S'], {0: 116, 1: 235}, <Invalid Chaid Split>),
   243	  (['male'], {0: 682, 1: 161}, (embarked, p=5.017855245e-05, score=16.4413525404, groups=[['C'], ['Q', 'S']]), dof=1)),
   244	  (['C'], {0: 109, 1: 48}, <Invalid Chaid Split>), (['Q', 'S'], {0: 573, 1: 113}, <Invalid Chaid Split>)
   245	]
   246	```
   247	
   248	So let's inspect the root node `tree.tree_store[0]`:
   249	
   250	``` python
   251	([], {0: 809, 1: 500}, (sex, p=1.47145310169e-81, score=365.886947811, groups=[['female'], ['male']]), dof=1))
   252	```
   253	
   254	Nodes have certain properties. Firstly, they show the column that was chosen to split to this node (for a root node the column is empty '([])'). The second property `{0: 809, 1: 500}` show the members of that node, and represent the current frequency of the dependent variable. In this case, it is all the answers in the 'survived' column, as that was the first column past to the program in the command line (`python -m CHAID tests/data/titanic.csv survived`). The next property represents the splitting of the node. What column was chosen to make that split (in this case, `sex`), the p-value of the split and the chi-score and most importantly, which variables in `sex` create the new nodes and the degrees of freedom associated with that split (1, in this case)
   255	
   256	These properties that can be accessed:
   257	
   258	``` python
   259	ipdb> root_node = tree.tree_store[0]
   260	ipdb> root_node.choices
   261	[]
   262	ipdb> root_node.members
   263	{0: 809, 1: 500}
   264	ipdb> root_node.split
   265	(sex, p=1.47145310169e-81, score=365.886947811, groups=[['female'], ['male']]), dof=1)
   266	```
   267	
   268	The split variable can be further inspected:
   269	
   270	``` python
   271	ipdb> split = root_node.split
   272	ipdb> split.column
   273	'sex'
   274	ipdb> split.p
   275	1.4714531016922664e-81
   276	ipdb> split.score
   277	365.88694781112048
   278	ipdb> split.dof
   279	1
   280	ipdb> split.groupings
   281	"[['female'], ['male']]"
   282	```
   283	
   284	Therefore, in this example, the root node is split on the column 'sex' in the data, splitting up the females and males. These females and males each form a new node and further down, the all male and all female nodes are split on the column 'embarked' (although they needn't split on the same column). A `<Invalid Chaid Split>` is reached when either the node is pure (only one dependent variable remains) or when a terminating parameter is met (e.g. min node size, or max depth [see tree parameters above])
   285	
   286	The conclusion drawn from this tree is that: "Gender was the most important factor driving the survival of people on the titanic. Whereby females had a much higher likelihood of surviving (survival = 1 in the survival column and 0 means they died). Of those females, those who embarked first class (class 'C', node 2) had a much higher likelihood of surviving."

   298	Caveats
   299	-------
   300	
   301	* Unlike SPSS, this library doesn't modify the data internally. This means that weight variables aren't rounded as they are in SPSS.
   302	* Every row is valid, even if all values are NaN or undefined. This is different to SPSS where in the weighted case it will strip out all rows if all the independent variables are NaN
   303	* All columns are currently treated as nominal
